Designing a near-optimal isolated microgrid using active learning
Cláudia Eliane da Matta a
 ,∗, Eliane Valença do Nascimento De Lorenci a,
João Alves da Silva Neto b, Antonio Carlos Zambroni de Souza a
 , Pedro Paulo Balestrassi a
a Universidade Federal de Itajubá - Unifei, Avenida BPS, 1303 - Pinheirinho, Itajubá, 37500-903, MG, Brazil
b Empresa de Pesquisa Energética - EPE, Praça Pio X, 54 - Centro, Rio de Janeiro, 20.040-020, RJ, Brazil
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Islanded microgrid network
Machine learning
Active learning
Active search
k-nearest neighbour regression
kNNR
Gaussian process regression
GPR
 A B S T R A C T
This paper proposes an innovative active-learning-based framework to identify near-optimal groupings of an 
islanded microgrid network. We aim to maximize service capacity and minimize total active power losses 
while maintaining voltage and frequency within operational constraints. Instead of exhaustive optimization, 
we adopt active learning to approximate optimal configurations, significantly reducing computational costs 
efficiently. The methodology involves designing a solution using machine learning techniques, implementing 
the solution computationally, and evaluating the benefits and limitations of the proposed approach. The results 
show that active search method efficiently identified the near-optimal microgrid grouping after evaluating only 
three configurations using both k-nearest neighbour regression and Gaussian process regression techniques. 
The method demonstrated superior computational efficiency while ensuring compliance with operational 
constraints.
1. Introduction
Microgrid systems represent an approach to decentralized energy 
generation, distribution, and consumption. As the global energy land-
scape shifts towards renewable sources and grid resilience, the role 
of microgrids becomes increasingly prominent [1]. These systems help 
optimize energy management, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and 
facilitate the integration of renewable resources into the electricity grid. 
However, achieving these objectives necessitates sophisticated control 
strategies that adapt to complex, often unpredictable environments [1].
As for the islanding process, this paper focuses on identifying an 
islanding configuration to extract the most from the existing sources. 
To this end, renewable sources may be employed [2], along with 
dispatchable generation. The strategy focused here seeks the best sin-
gle configuration following a disconnection from the grid. It differs 
from [3], where a dynamic island forming is proposed.
Such a methodology allows the configuration to change over time. 
The strategy proposed in this paper may emulate this characteristic if 
each period of interest is considered as an islanding interval.
In real-world applications, absolute optimality is often impractical 
due to computational constraints. This study employs active learning 
techniques to achieve near-optimal solutions for efficiently clustering 
islanded microgrids. By iteratively selecting promising configurations 
through machine learning predictions, the method rapidly converges

In this context, this paper proposes a machine learning approach 
that uses active learning to define a near-optimal islanded microgrid 
clustering aimed at maximizing service capacity. The term active is 
used herein because the search method interacts with the analyst by 
indicating the objects subjected to the direct analysis procedure. This 
concept bears similarity with active learning techniques [4], which 
have been studied within the scope of classification [5,6] and multi-
variate calibration tasks [7]. However, such active learning techniques 
are aimed at the construction of classification or regression models. In 
contrast, the present work concerns an optimization problem, which 
does not necessarily involve constructing an explicit model.
The regression techniques applied here are a k-nearest-neighbour 
method [8] and a Gaussian process [9]. The algorithm searches for the 
most promising object with the best features for building a model. It 
was applied to a modified IEEE 37-node test feeder in order to define 
the best clustering for the network under islanded mode.
The contributions of this paper are:
• Proposing an intelligent algorithm to define a near-optimal clus-
tering for an islanded microgrid to maximize service capacity.

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. The Sec-
tion 2 presents a brief review of microgrid operation in islanded mode. 
The Section 3 describes the proposed search method based on active 
machine learning. The Section 4 describes simulation results and dis-
cussions. In the conclusion, the final considerations of this research are 
presented.
2. Microgrid operation in islanded mode
2.1. Inverter operation mode
This section discusses different ways of operating a microgrid in 
isolated mode. Distributed generators are connected to the grid by an 
inverter-based interface [10]. This paper assumes two possible control 
modes for the operation of the inverter during the islanded condition, 
given by PQ control mode and Voltage Source Inverter (VSI) control 
mode.
Renewable energy sources such as photovoltaic systems are con-
trolled by PQ mode and, hence, are considered as negative power 
loads. The VSI mode is used for dispatchable generators (such as 
microturbines). Since the frequency and voltage are dependent upon 
the demand, the active and reactive powers generated at the unit (𝑃𝑔𝑘
and 𝑄𝑔𝑘 , respectively) are given by droop control equations, as depicted

3. Proposed methodology
The proposed methodology is grounded in the active machine learn-
ing paradigm, specifically active search, which aims to identify high-
performing solutions with a limited number of evaluations. The active 
learning strategy employed does not perform an exhaustive search of 
the entire solution space, hence it does not strictly guarantee global 
optimality. Instead, the methodology iteratively approximates opti-
mal solutions by evaluating only the most informative configurations 
suggested by surrogate models, resulting in efficient convergence to 
practically near-optimal outcomes.
3.1. Problem description
In this article, the concept of microgrid clustering is applied in 
the context of islanded operation. The concept of microgrid clustering 
consists of dividing a system into smaller subsystems. In this context, 
the microgrid is divided into multiple islands that can be grouped, 
forming different clusters.
It is assumed that a microgrid can be divided into smaller units, 
referred to as submicrogrids, as depicted in Fig.  1, which shows a

These smaller microgrids can be grouped into different arrangements, 
each referred to as a cluster, where microgrids 1 to 6 are represented 
by M1, M2, M3, M4, M5, and M6, respectively. Multiple clusters can 
be organized into different groupings. Table  1 shows the 32 possible 
groupings derived from the submicrogrids in Fig.  1.
In this work, it is considered that the time of disconnection from the 
main grid and the amount of time that the system will stay disconnected 
are known. From a planning perspective, the proposed methodology 
aims to determine the grouping that, for a specified period of disconnec-
tion, has the maximum service capacity. This is the grouping where all 
clusters maintain the frequency and voltage levels within operational 
limits and minimizes total losses. One strategy to assess the service 
capacity of the different groupings is to perform a power flow analysis 
over the specific period of disconnection, for each possible cluster. Note 
that, in the study, both load and photovoltaic generation profiles during 
the disconnection hours are considered, and the microturbine output 
follows the droop control (Eqs. (1) and (2)). Thus, the methodology 
takes advantage of primary control, which requires no communication 
among the generating units.
The strategy previously described is associated with high compu-
tational cost, as the number of clusters requiring power flow analysis 
increases with the penetration of distributed generation and the geo-
graphical extent of the microgrid. In this context, as part of the planning 
process, this work proposes an intelligent algorithm based on active 
search to define the near-optimal microgrid clustering for islanded 
operation. The AI-based methodology eliminates the need to perform 
power flow analysis for all possible clusters; instead, the analysis is 
limited to a reduced set of promising groupings.
For this purpose, this article proposes a novel methodological frame-
work for microgrids that leverages machine learning to determine the 
near-optimal grouping of an islanded microgrid network, aiming to 
maximize service capacity during islanded operation while satisfying 
operational constraints such as voltage and frequency limits.
Operational constraints — frequency within [59.5 Hz, 60 Hz] and 
voltage within acceptable IEEE standard ranges (0.95–1.05 p.u.) — 
are explicitly evaluated at each iteration through detailed power flow 
simulations. Surrogate models predict active power losses to select 
promising candidates, but the feasibility check (compliance with oper-
ational constraints) is performed rigorously via these simulations. Any 
candidate violating these constraints is deemed infeasible, and thus 
excluded from the selection as a near-optimal solution.
In the context of this study, a near-optimal grouping refers to a 
configuration of islanded microgrids partitioned into clusters that oper-
ate in coordination to maximize service capacity and/or minimize total 
active power losses, while satisfying system constraints such as voltage 
and frequency limits. Each grouping represents a unique combination 
of microgrids that are temporarily interconnected to form one or more 
autonomous clusters during the disconnection period. Optimality is 
evaluated based on the grouping’s ability to supply loads, ensure oper-
ational stability, and reduce electrical losses in the network. Therefore, 
‘‘near-optimal grouping’’ is not a topological or graph-theoretical con-
cept in this context, but rather a practical operational strategy derived 
from the evaluation and comparison of multiple possible combinations 
of microgrid clusters under power system constraints.
3.2. Objective function
In this study, the objective function 𝑦 represents the total active 
power loss in a given microgrid grouping during islanded operation, 
which must be minimized. The loss is computed as the sum of the losses 
in each cluster that forms the group, based on power flow calculation.
Operational constraints were defined clearly to reflect realistic is-
landed conditions: frequency constraints ([59.5 Hz, 60 Hz]) explicitly 
target the most common islanded scenario—frequency drops due to 
generation deficits following grid disconnection. IEEE 1547-2018 [15] 
specifies broader ranges, including transient overfrequency limits (up 
to approximately 60.5 Hz), but this study emphasizes underfrequency 
conditions common in isolated operational scenarios. Similarly, volt-
age constraints are defined explicitly within ±5% of nominal values

3.3. Active learning
In many analytical applications, the problem consists of finding an 
object with an optimal or near-optimal value for a specific y-property 
of interest within a given pool of objects [16].
Active learning aims to select a reduced and non-redundant pair to 
produce a training set with information that faithfully represents an 
unlabelled dataset [17]. An active search is essentially an optimization 
strategy based on active machine learning, in which new experimental 
data is selected iteratively to find an experiment that optimizes the 
objective. It is considered an area of active machine learning and it is 
a method proposed in the literature to find the optimal of objective 
functions that are costly to evaluate. Besides, this technique aims 
to minimize the number of objective function evaluations. It applies 
when there is no closed expression for the objective function, but 
observations of that function can be obtained from the sampled values.
This system applies an active search method to find objects with 
optimal or near-optimal 𝑦-values based on 𝑐-components obtained 
through indirect and less costly methods. The search algorithm pro-
gresses sequentially, starting from a small subset of objects with known 
𝑦-values. At each iteration, a multivariate weighted-averaging tech-
nique — k-nearest neighbour regression (kNNR) or Gaussian process 
regression (GPR) — is employed to estimate ̂ 𝑦-values for objects with 
unknown 𝑦-values. The object with the best ̂ 𝑦-value is selected as the 
most likely candidate for optimality. This candidate is then subjected 
to a direct analysis procedure to evaluate the 𝑦-property.
3.3.1. Kennard–Stone algorithm
The initialization procedure is carried out using the Kennard–Stone 
(KS) algorithm, which is a classical method for selecting objects in 
a near-uniform manner based on the Euclidean distances between 
each pair of 𝐱-vectors [18]. This method is initialized by selecting 𝑛0
objects based on the 𝐱-vectors alone, i.e., without using any information 
concerning the associated 𝑦-values. The first two selected objects are 
separated by the most considerable distance in the x-space. Each sub-
sequent object is chosen according to a maximum–minimum procedure 
to avoid selecting objects that are close together.
The KS algorithm selects an initial subset of microgrid configu-
rations with maximum geometric dispersion in the input space. The 
first two points selected are those with the largest Euclidean distance 
between them, and subsequent points are added iteratively to maximize 
the minimum distance to already-selected points. This ensures that the 
initial sample is representative of the diversity of the entire solution 
space, which is crucial for training effective surrogate models in the 
early stages of the active search.
3.3.2. K-nearest neighbour regression
The method kNNR is a type of machine learning algorithm that is 
robust, simple to implement, and computationally inexpensive [19,20]. 
The number of neighbours to interpolate over, 𝑘, is user-specified, and 
the 𝑘 training points with the smallest Euclidean distance in the input 
feature space are defined as nearest. Thus, kNNR can predict an output 
value by taking a weighted average of data points with similar input 
features.

3.3.3. Gaussian process regression
GPR can be seen as a Bayesian nonparametric approach to regres-
sion, where the function from the Gaussian processes takes values in 
a function space [11]. As in the previous case, it is assumed that the 
initial objects were selected using the KS algorithm and that a total of 
𝑛 ≤ 𝑛𝑚𝑎𝑥 objects are selected at the end of the active search.
As the active search aims to improve the accuracy, remaining 
sensitive to the optimization costs. Thus, it was necessary to define 
a criterion by calculating the confidence intervals for the estimated 
values ̂ 𝑦. After the training, the prediction of the ̂ 𝑦-values for the 
unselected objects is made, and the index of the object with the highest 
value of ̂ 𝑦 is selected. Next, the confidence interval is tested. If the 
algorithm does not find a confidence interval value greater than the 
𝑦-value already selected, the algorithm is terminated. For this study, 
the 95% confidence interval was considered
For the GPR model, we adopted the squared exponential kernel 
with Automatic Relevance Determination (ARD), as implemented in 
MATLAB® (‘‘ardsquaredexponential’’). This kernel automatically tunes 
the length-scale hyperparameters for each input dimension, enhancing 
model flexibility and precision in high-dimensional spaces. Hyperpa-
rameters were optimized using the log marginal likelihood maximiza-
tion method available in the MATLAB regression learner. Additionally, 
to reduce computational burden during iterative retraining, we im-
plemented a stopping criterion based on the confidence interval of 
predictions: if the upper bound of the confidence interval for a candi-
date configuration was lower than the best observed value, the search 
was terminated early.

4. Simulation results and discussions
This paper uses active search to determining a near-optimal group-
ing for an island microgrid network aimed at maximizing service 
capacity. The network is divided into six microgrids (Fig.  1) in which 
active search studies are carried out. Each microgrid corresponds to 
a standard radial distribution system. Depending on the connections 
available, the microgrids can be grouped, forming multiple clusters, 
which, in turn, can be further arranged in cluster groups, as shown 
in Table  1. In normal operation, the microgrids are connected to the 
main system. For the simulations carried out, it is assumed that the 
microgrids are isolated from the main electricity system as a function of 
a disconnection from the main grid, and disconnection time is known. 
Also, the maximum power supplied is known, which is considered by 
the methodology to manage the energy supply during the island mode 
of operation.
This work presents dispatchable energy sources on Buses 725, 729, 
731, 225, 229 and 231. On the other hand, non-dispatchable units 
have variable energy generation since the energy source is intermittent 
and dependent on weather conditions. The main examples of non-
dispatchable units are wind and solar generation. This work uses only 
photovoltaic generation as an intermittent energy source at Buses 
724, 742, 224, and 242. Notice that Microgrids 3 and 4 only have 
dispatchable energy sources.
The disconnection time directly affects the management of the 
available energy and, ultimately, the system’s ability to meet the load 
demand. The proposed algorithm is designed to account for this char-
acteristic. In this context, islands are formed based on all possible 
combinations of the previously created mini-microgrids. The identi-
fication of near-optimal groupings is performed by the active search 
algorithm.
The study considers the disconnection of the microgrids from the 
main system, and each microgrid’s predicted energy generation is 
assumed. The base power adopted is 2.5 kVA, so a generation of, for 
example, 2 p.u.h corresponds to 5 kWh.
4.1. Proposed framework
The proposed framework, as can be seen in Fig.  3, consists of 
4 phases: (1) specification of all possible microgrid groupings, (2) 
definition of the problem components, (3) correlation analysis and (4) 
application of the active search algorithm to find the near-optimal 
grouping of microgrids.
Phase 1: In this phase, the six islanded microgrids (Table  1) can be 
combined into 32 different groupings. In this table, the first column in-
dicates the grouping number, while the subsequent columns correspond 
to clusters 1 through 6. It should be noted that each grouping consists 
of one or more clusters (up to six), and each cluster may contain one 
or more microgrids (up to six). For example, Grouping 1 represents a 
single cluster containing all six microgrids.
Phase 2: Each grouping described in Table  1 corresponds to an 
object, which is made of components: the energy generated and the 
energy demanded by each cluster. For a better understanding, Table  2 
(ID 2) describes an example of object configuration, which relates to 
Grouping 2.
Phase 3: The correlation of the components was analysed and the 
components with high correlation are removed. Thus, the components 
𝑐2, 𝑐4, 𝑐6, 𝑐8, 𝑐10 and 𝑐12 were removed from the objects, leaving 5 
components, 𝑐1, 𝑐3, 𝑐5, 𝑐7, 𝑐9 and 𝑐11 which correspond to the energy 
generated from the clusters 1–6.
Phase 4: Active search is used to find the grouping with the highest 
energy availability to serve the loads when the system is isolated, 
i.e., the grouping with the lowest total loss, with all clusters operating 
within the allowed frequency range (59.5 Hz ≤ 𝑓 𝑟𝑒𝑞 ≤ 60 Hz ). In the 
simulations, calculating the total loss of each grouping requires solving 
the power flow during the period of disconnection for each cluster 
within the grouping: the total loss corresponds to the sum of the losses 
of each cluster.
4.2. Defining the near-optimal microgrid clustering for islanded operation
The initial number of training objects (groupings) was determined 
using the KS algorithm. A value of 𝑛0 = 2 (initial objects) was chosen. 
The values of the property of interest (𝑦), which correspond to the total 
loss, are then computed for the two selected objects by solving the 
power flow for each of the corresponding groupings. It is important to 
note that power flow calculations are not performed for the remaining 
objects. Additionally, the frequency associated with each cluster of 
these groupings is derived from the solution of the power flow problem. 
These objects are subsequently used to train the regression model 
(kNNR or GPR).
Next, the adjusted regression model is applied to calculate ̂ 𝑦 (es-
timated value for property of interest) for the 30 remaining objects. 
The object with the highest ̂ 𝑦 is selected, and its corresponding 𝑦 value 
is calculated, meaning that the power flow calculation is performed 
for this object (or grouping). This object is then incorporated into the 
training set of the regression model.
In the third iteration, the regression model is updated with the three 
objects (those for which the power flow was calculated in previous 
iterations) to estimate ̂ 𝑦 for the remaining 29 objects. This process is 
repeated until a stopping criterion is met. The stopping criterion is 
determined by calculating the confidence intervals for the estimated 
̂ 𝑦 values. For this study, a 95% confidence interval was considered. 
If the ̂ 𝑦 interval does not exceed the 𝑦 values of the objects already 
selected, the object is added to the training set; otherwise, the algorithm 
terminates. This criterion was met after the ninth iteration, as indicated 
by the red dashed line, as shown in Figs.  4(a) and 4(b). In this 
case, the active search method for determining microgrid groupings 
quickly identified the near-optimal grouping. In contrast, when no 
search method is used, the near-optimal grouping is only identified in 
the 22nd iteration.
Fig.  4(a) compares the kNNR active search (kNNR AS) method 
with the no-search method. The kNNR AS technique (as outlined in 
Algorithm 1) is then used to estimate the total loss for each microgrid 
grouping that has not yet been selected. The grouping with the lowest 
estimated total loss, which also satisfies the defined constraint, is 
subsequently chosen. In this case, this was identified during the third 
iteration. The GPR active search (GPR AS) is then used to estimate the 
total loss for each microgrid grouping that have not yet been selected, 
similar to kNNR AS. In this case, this microgrid grouping with the 
lowest total was found during the third interaction. Fig.  4(b) compares 
the results obtained for active search using the GPR technique and 
no-search method.
The grouping with the least energy loss was identified by the active 
search method when evaluating the third object using both the kNNR 
AS and GPR AS techniques. This grouping corresponds to object 22. In 
this study, the better solution was reached after only three iterations.

The active search method significantly reduced the number of it-

the load demand within the established frequency, while minimizing 
total loss. It is important to note that the value of the property of 
interest, in the case of microgrids, was achieved after a limited number 
of iterations, thereby reducing the number of control system operations 
needed to execute the power flow calculations.

voltage limits) verified through detailed power flow simulations. Thus, 
this configuration not only minimizes total active power losses but 
also ensures compliance with critical operational requirements. In this 
configuration, Microgrids 1 and 6 are isolated, while Microgrids 2–3 
and 4–5 are grouped together.

While the initialization of kNNR and GPR is essentially similar, the 
main differences and advantages lie in the model training. The basic 
principle and process of kNNR are not considered complex, as they 
rely on a distance-based criterion to estimate the value of 𝑦. On the 
other hand, GPR incorporates a Bayesian model during the training 
process, providing a probabilistic framework for making predictions 
and quantifying uncertainty.
In the kNNR technique, the parameter 𝑘 used to estimate the prop-
erty 𝑦 is a design variable that must be selected by the researcher. Good 
results were also obtained using a simpler version of this technique, in 
which all the selected objects are used to estimate 𝑦. In contrast, GPR is 
highly dependent on the hyperparameters of its kernel function, which 
vary according to the nature of the data, making the algorithm more 
adaptable than kNNR.
The time to find the best scenario using kNNR AS was 0.106 ms 
and using GPR AS was 1.643 ms, within a MATLAB® programming 
environment. The tests were carried out on a computer with an Intel®
Core i7-6700, Central Processing Unit (CPU) 3.41 GHz, with 4 GB 
of Random Access Memory (RAM) installed, using the Windows® 10 
Education operating system.
Metaheuristic optimization techniques, such as Particle Swarm Op-
timization (PSO) and Genetic Algorithms (GA) are widely used for 
constrained optimization problems, including microgrid planning and 
reconfiguration. However, they typically require a large number of 
objective function evaluations to converge. When applied to scenarios 
that involve repeated power flow simulations, these techniques can 
become computationally prohibitive, especially during planning stages 
or in real-time applications. In contrast, the basic principle and process 
of kNNR AS are not considered complex, as they rely on a distance-
based criterion to estimate the value of 𝑦. The number 𝑘 used to 
estimate the property 𝑦 is a design parameter that must be chosen by 
the researcher.
The GPR incorporates a Bayesian model during the training process, 
providing a probabilistic framework for making predictions and quan-
tifying uncertainty. GPR is highly dependent on the hyperparameters 
of its kernel function, which vary according to the nature of the data, 
making the algorithm more adaptable than kNNR.
Although the experimental validation in this study focuses on com-
parisons with the KS selection method, it is important to contextualize 
the proposed methodology in relation to other clustering and optimiza-
tion techniques commonly found in the literature. To this end, Table  3 
presents a comparative summary of different active learning methods, 
including PSO and GA. The comparison encompasses aspects such 
as model complexity, parameter tuning, interpretability, adaptability, 
average number of iterations, and source of information. The data 
for PSO and GA are drawn from published studies addressing similar 
microgrid optimization scenarios.
The GA demonstrates strong performance in addressing high-
dimensional and nonlinear optimization problems, due to its population-
based evolutionary structure, which promotes a broad search space 
exploration and reduces the likelihood of being trapped in local optima. 
This makes GA particularly effective for the optimization of hybrid 
microgrid systems that integrate multiple distributed energy resources 
and require simultaneous consideration of environmental and eco-
nomic objectives [21,22]. In contrast, PSO operates through relatively 
simple update mechanisms involving particle velocity and position, 
which results in a lower computational burden compared to GA [23]. 
However, advanced PSO variants, particularly those integrating adap-
tive inertia weights or constriction factors, have exhibited superior 
ability to balance exploration and exploitation. Consequently, these 
approaches attain performance levels comparable to GA in solving com-
plex optimization problems, all while preserving higher convergence 
efficiency [24].
Therefore, although this study does not offer an exhaustive nu-
merical comparison with all existing methods, the proposed approach 
demonstrates strong advantages in terms of computational efficiency, 
robustness, and practical applicability in constrained power system 
optimization problems.
In this paper, we systematically explain for the first time how 
active learning can be applied to determining near-optimal groupings 
of islanded microgrids. The results of these studies demonstrate that 
the active search method holds significant potential for addressing this 
problem.
5. Conclusion
This work developed a structured approach to determine a near-
optimal grouping for an islanded microgrid network, aiming to maxi-
mize service capacity through an active-learning paradigm and mini-
mize the number of simulations.
Primary control was employed based on the droop method, and 
an islanding technique has been proposed to optimize the system 
configuration so that the load supply is maximized while preserving 
the operating constraints. The methodology proposed may provide 
dynamic islanding formation and manage the energy available as a 
function of the disconnection time.
This article proposes an innovative approach and presents the fol-
lowing key findings. First, the study successfully applies microgrid 
clustering to enhance service capacity during disconnection from the 
main electricity grid. Second, the active-search method significantly re-
duces the number of iterations required to determine the near-optimal

5.1. Limitations of the current work and suggestions for future investigation
While the proposed method efficiently identifies high-performance, 
practically viable solutions, it does not guarantee global optimality 
due to its reliance on predictive surrogate modelling. Thus, the results 
are appropriately categorized as near-optimal, well-suited for prac-
tical microgrid operational planning where computational efficiency 
and quick response are priorities. Despite the method’s demonstrating 
high efficiency and effectiveness in identifying near-optimal microgrid 
groupings under islanded conditions, it is important to acknowledge 
some limitations:
• No optimized hyperparameters of the Gaussian process regres-
sion: The difficulty in configuring these hyperparameters stems 
from the wide range of possibilities they offer. For future work, it 
is recommended to explore methods to optimize these parameters.
• No real-time reconfiguration: The method is designed for pre-
planning, not real-time operation. Integrating it with real-time 
control systems would require additional layers of
decision-making and validation.
• No explicit failure scenarios: The method assumes full availability 
of the microgrid infrastructure. Modelling grid component fail-
ures (e.g., line faults, inverter shutdowns) would enhance the 
robustness of the optimization strategy.
